newsitem.title: UK: London and Dublin agree on IRA arms issue - Bruton.
newsitem.headline: London and Dublin agree on IRA arms issue - Bruton.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Monday that London and Dublin had agreed a joint stance on guerrilla disarmament that could pave the way for progress in deadlocked Northern Ireland peace talks, Irish television reported.

Bruton announced the move in New York after an unscheduled meeting with his British counterpart, Tony Blair, who was in the United States for a meeting of the Group of Seven nations with Russia, and then the United Nations Earth Summit.
Irish network RTE quoted Bruton as saying the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in current peace talks.

It said the accord dealt with ways to bring about the disarmament of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting to end British rule in the territory, if the guerrillas called an end to long-running violence.

An Anglo-Irish paper aimed at ending a 17-month stalemate between Protestant and Catholic politicians at multi-party talks on "arms decommissioning" was expected to be tabled in Belfast on Tuesday, political sources said.
According to RTE, Bruton said that all possible clarification had now been provided to Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA.
He said Sinn Fein now had to choose between the political path and the dual approach of political action and violence that it had been pursuing.
Sinn Fein is barred from the multi-party discussions because the IRA refuses to restore a truce it broke in February 1996.
Earlier Sinn Fein's chief negotiator Martin McGuinness had said the disarmament issue remained a major stumbling block in peace efforts.
He said Sinn Fein wanted an end to violence in the province and the start of real peace negotiations.

"We are working day and night...trying to move the situation forward, and to convince the British government and others that the decommissioning issue which has blocked this process must be removed as an obstacle to forward movement," he told BBC radio.
Republicans opposed to British rule have always maintained that the IRA will not call a ceasefire if they suspect the negotiations will be turned into a "decommissioning conference".
Britain says it will not permit Sinn Fein and the IRA to hold the peace process to ransom.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam on Monday dismissed Sinn Fein protests that the peace process was being stymied by demands for arms to be scrapped.
"I think Sinn Fein ought to be concentrating on giving me an unequivocal ceasefire before they tell me what else I should be doing," she told reporters in the city of Londonderry.

Separately, Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams urged nationalists to be on alert for attacks by pro-British "Loyalists", saying police had warned some 12 Catholics in west Belfast that they were in danger from Protestant pro-British extremists.
"There have been consistent reports of recent months of loyalist death squads targeting republicans," Adams said in a statement.
A police spokeswoman said persons had called on a number of homes to "advise members of the public in relation to their personal security". She declined to give further details.
The IRA's murder of two police patrolmen last week, which was followed by two suspected Protestant bomb attacks on Catholics, has clouded hopes of political progress.
The killings also increased fears of sectarian violence during the usually volatile marching season.

Blair, who severed low-level contacts with Sinn Fein last week after the IRA killings, was expected to make a parliamentary statement on Wednesday on the terms, based on an end to violence, for Sinn Fein to enter talks.

Political sources said the Anglo-Irish agreement on scrapping arms is likely to mirror proposals by the talks' chairman, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, for the issue to be tackled alongside negotiations on other political matters.
